In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the histopathological findings and chemokine profiles of LNs in patients with AODS are distinctive from those of other mimickers, and may be useful in differentiating AODS from other conditions.
the histopathological and immunohistochemical findings in LNs of AOSD are characterized by paracortex hyperplasia with immunoblasts, histiocytes, and CD8-positive lymphocytes.

the histopathologic findings, immunohistochemical staining, and clinical manifestations of AOSD are useful to differentiate AOSD from T cell lymphoma and HNL, which is a rare systemic autoimmune disease.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
AOSD is associated with a unique chemokine profile in the lymph nodes.
AOSD is an immune-mediated systemic inflammatory disease that is characterized by lymphadenopathy and chemokine overexpression in LNs, which may be related to the pathogenesis.
AOSD is characterized by paracortex hyperplasia with immunoblast proliferation and expression of chemokines, which may play an important role in the pathogenesis of AOSD.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the chemokines, especially CXCL10 and S100A9, are involved in the pathogenesis of AOSD and may serve as biomarkers for diagnosis.
CXCL10 and its receptor, CXCR3 are expressed at high levels in LNs of patients with AODS.
CXCL10, and CXCR-3 expression may aid in the diagnosis of adult onset Still's disease.
